name: OpenAI's HealthBench: a physician-built benchmark for AI in healthcare
title: OpenAI's HealthBench: a physician-built benchmark for AI in healthcare
answer: OpenAI's HealthBench is a benchmark for measuring AI capability in health, built with 262 physicians practising across 60 countries. It contains 5,000 realistic health conversations, each graded by a custom physician-written rubric, giving 48,562 unique criteria covering themes such as emergency situations, handling uncertainty and global health. It is the clearest public yardstick for judging whether a model is fit for clinical work.

sections.body: This is OpenAI's announcement page for HealthBench, published on openai.com and read on 3 October 2026. It is a product and research announcement rather than a clinical guideline or a peer-reviewed paper. Its scope is the design and construction of the benchmark: who built it, how the conversations and grading criteria were assembled, and how responses are scored. It describes the benchmark itself rather than reporting results for any particular model, and it is published by the organisation whose models the benchmark is intended to assess.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: HealthBench is a benchmark for measuring AI capabilities in health, built in partnership with 262 physicians who have practised in 60 countries. It contains 5,000 realistic health conversations, and each conversation carries a custom rubric written by a physician to grade model responses. Across the set there are 48,562 unique rubric criteria. Responses are not scored by the physicians who wrote the rubrics but by a model-based grader, GPT-4.1. The conversations are divided into seven themes, which the page illustrates with emergency situations, handling uncertainty and global health. Every rubric criterion carries an axis defining what aspect of model behaviour it grades, such as accuracy, communication quality or context seeking. The examples were created over the past year by the physician group, who between them are proficient in 49 languages and hold training in 26 medical specialties. The listed languages range from English, Mandarin Chinese, Spanish and Arabic to Afaan Oromo, Chichewa, Dzongkha, Kikuyu, Luo, Tumbuka and Twi. The listed specialties include emergency medicine, family medicine, internal medicine, diagnostic radiology, neurology, paediatrics, psychiatry, obstetrics and gynaecology, general surgery and public health.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that HealthBench was built with 262 physicians who have practised in 60 countries; that it contains 5,000 realistic health conversations; that these carry 48,562 unique rubric criteria; that responses are graded by GPT-4.1 as a model-based grader; that conversations fall into seven themes; and that the contributing physicians are proficient in 49 languages and trained in 26 medical specialties.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in healthcare, this source matters because it describes an evaluation instrument rather than a product claim. The design choices it records are the ones that decide what a clinical benchmark actually measures: conversations drawn from realistic practice, rubrics written by practising physicians rather than by the model vendor's engineers, criteria tagged by axis so that accuracy can be separated from communication quality and context seeking, and coverage spread across languages and specialties rather than concentrated in English-language primary care. The breadth of the physician panel, spanning 60 countries, 49 languages and 26 specialties, is the source's own answer to the charge that health benchmarks over-represent a single health system. A reader can use the page to understand what a clinical model score means before citing it.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Healthcare

sections.body: The page is an announcement by the organisation whose models are being assessed, so it is promotional in origin even where it is technical. It describes how the benchmark was built but does not report scores for any named model, so it cannot be used to compare systems. Grading is delegated to a model-based grader, GPT-4.1, a choice the page states without discussing its accuracy or failure modes. The page gives no release date for the benchmark, no licensing or access terms, and no detail on how the seven themes are weighted or how conversations were sampled.
